books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

primary_sources: Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825

stimulus.text: “Mr. Adams is the Constitutional President and as such I would myself be the last man in the Commonwealth to oppose him upon any other ground than that of principle. How he reached the office is an enquiry for the succeeding canvass, when the principles of the Constitution, apart from his ministerial acts, or at least without necessary opposition to them, will sanction the investigation.” — Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825.
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825. Verbatim quotation; wording verified against the Library of Congress citation of the letter. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Jackson accepts Adams as president yet promises an investigation at “the succeeding canvass.” What does that pairing show about Jackson's strategy?

options.text: He accepted the legal result while keeping the corruption charge alive for 1828
He planned to overturn the election by force
options.misconception: Jackson says he would be the last man to oppose Adams except on principle; he promises a campaign, not a revolt.

options.text: He admitted that the charge of a corrupt bargain against Adams was false
options.misconception: He says the opposite: the way Adams reached office is a question to be investigated.

options.text: He asked Congress to annul the election
options.misconception: Jackson looks to the next canvass, the voters, not to Congress undoing the result.

rationales.A: Calling Adams the Constitutional President concedes the office, while saving the question for the next campaign keeps the “corrupt bargain” charge working for four years.
rationales.B: Jackson promises an investigation at the next canvass, not force.
rationales.C: He keeps the charge open; he never says it was false.
rationales.D: He appeals to the voters at the next election, not to Congress.
rationales.general:
1. Split the sentence. The first half concedes the office; the second half keeps the charge.
2. Ask what each half does. Conceding the office keeps Jackson lawful, while the promised investigation keeps his supporters angry.
3. Follow it to 1828. Jackson ran the next campaign as the people's candidate against an elite bargain.
Background: The House had chosen Adams though Jackson won the most popular and electoral votes, so the charge had real sting.
Remember: a smart loser concedes the office and contests the story.
